ORIGINAL ARTICLE: Clinical Endoscopy

A prospective evaluation of fatty pancreas by using EUS
Paul S. Sepe, MD, Ashray Ohri, Sirish Sanaka, MD, Tyler M. Berzin, MD, Sandeep Sekhon, MD,
Gayle Bennett, MD, Gaurav Mehta, MD, Ram Chuttani, MD, Robert Kane, MD, Douglas Pleskow, MD,
Mandeep S. Sawhney, MD
Boston, Massachusetts, USA

Background: Fatty liver is associated with obesity, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and the metabolic syndrome. The
pathophysiology of fatty pancreas is poorly understood, but it may be closely related to fatty liver.
Objective: The aim of our study was to determine the prevalence of fatty pancreas and risk factors associated
with its development.
Design: Prospective, single center study.
Setting: Tertiary-care academic medical center.
Patients: This study involved 250 consecutive patients referred for EUS examination.
Intervention: All patients undergoing EUS at our institution were prospectively identified. Information regarding
demographics, tobacco use, alcohol use, blood test results, and comorbidities were collected before EUS. Pancreatic
echogenicity was graded in comparison to the spleen at the time of EUS by using an a priori specified grading scheme.
Main Outcome Measurements: Prevalence of fatty pancreas and factors associated with its development.
Results: During the study period, 250 consecutive patients were prospectively enrolled. The prevalence of fatty
pancreas was 27.8% (95% CI, 22.1-34.1). Fatty liver was seen in 22.6% of patients. Factors associated with fatty
pancreas on univariate analysis were increasing body mass index (BMI) (P ⫽ .004), fatty liver (P ⬍ .0001),
hyperlipidemia (P ⫽ .04), and the metabolic syndrome (odds ratio [OR] 3.13, P ⫽ .004). The presence of any
metabolic syndrome components, that is, BMI ⱖ30, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, or hypertension, increased the
prevalence of fatty pancreas by 37% (OR 1.37, P ⫽ .01). Factors independently associated with fatty pancreas on
multivariate analysis were increasing BMI (OR 1.05, P ⫽ .03) and fatty liver (OR 3.61, P ⬍ .001). We found no
association between fatty pancreas and chronic pancreatitis or adenocarcinoma of the pancreas.
Limitations: Single institution study. All patients were referred for EUS, which limits generalizability. Lack of
histological confirmation of pancreatic fat.
Conclusion: We found a strong association between fatty pancreas and the metabolic syndrome. (Gastrointest
Endosc 2011;73:987-93.)

Obesity has become one of the most important health
problems in the United States, affecting more than onethird of the population.1 Associated comorbidities include

hypertension, diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, cardiovascular disease, and the metabolic syndrome. The importance of both visceral and ectopic fat as an endocrine organ

that secretes multiple adipokines has been appreciated.2-4
Under conditions of oxidative stress, this cytokine milieu
has been demonstrated to produce a local inflammatory
response and organ dysfunction. This has been most studied in the liver, where fat deposition in hepatocytes has
been shown to lead to nonalcoholic fatty liver disease and
nonalcoholic steatohepatitis.5 Pancreatic steatosis also has
been demonstrated, but its pathophysiologic consequences are much less understood. It has been suggested
that a similar process of nonalcoholic fatty pancreas disease and nonalcoholic steatopancreatitis occurs. This has
led some to hypothesize that pancreatic steatosis may
promote the development of chronic pancreatitis and cancer, exacerbate the severity of acute pancreatitis, increase
the risk of pancreatic surgery, and lead to B-cell dysfunction and the development of type II diabetes mellitus.3,4
Several studies have attempted to further evaluate this
entity. Older autopsy and transabdominal US series have
suggested age and body mass index (BMI) as associated
variables,6-9 whereas more recent studies have demonstrated additional possible associations including hepatic
steatosis, alcohol use, visceral fat, insulin resistance, alanine aminotransferase levels, B-cell dysfunction, and
diabetes.10-16 These studies were limited by small sample
size and retrospective design. The aim of our study was
to prospectively determine the prevalence of pancreatic
steatosis and to identify risk factors associated with its
development. We hypothesized that fatty pancreas was
more prevalent than previously recognized and was
associated with the metabolic syndrome and its associated components.

Take-home Message
Pancreatic steatosis is noted in 1 in 4 patients undergoing
EUS. Obesity, hepatic steatosis, and increasing number of
metabolic syndrome parameters are predictive of
pancreatic steatosis.
● There appears to be a strong association between
pancreatic steatosis and the metabolic syndrome.
●

All patients who underwent EUS at Beth Israel Deaconess
Medical Center from October 2009 to January 2010 were
prospectively enrolled. Patient demographics, tobacco/
alcohol use, and comorbidities were recorded by using a data
collection instrument designed for this study. We recorded
history of diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. Patients met criteria for these if they reported such a diagnosis and were either (1) on medications for treatment or
(2) were not on medications but primary care records
confirmed such a diagnosis. We also recorded history of
pancreatic adenocarcinoma and acute and chronic pancreatitis as well as all medications used for ⬎6 weeks over the
previous year. Medical records were reviewed in all cases
to confirm these. Tobacco use was quantified as pack
years (packs of cigarettes smoked per day times number of
years). Alcohol use was quantified as the ethanol index
(alcoholic drinks per week times number of years). If
quantity of tobacco or alcohol use differed by time period,
pack years or ethanol index was averaged over time. Low
density lipoprotein, high density lipoprotein, total cholesterol, triglycerides, amylase, and lipase levels were re-

corded from the medical record if they were available
within 1 year of the EUS examination. The metabolic
syndrome was defined by using a modified version of the
International Diabetes Federation definition.17 This included BMI ⱖ30 and any 2 of the following 3 comorbidities: diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, as determined by standard clinical or laboratory test parameters.
EUS was performed by using a linear or radial array
echoendoscope in standard fashion. All studies were done
with the Olympus Aloka 5 processor (Olympus America
Inc, Center Valley, Penn). Pancreatic parenchyma was
examined and echogenicity was prospectively graded I
through IV at the time of EUS by one of two experienced
endosonographers (M.S., D.P.). The classification system
was adapted from that used by Marks et al7 and Worthen
and Beabeau.9 In addition to assessment of pancreatic
echogenicity, we also assessed the pancreas for clarity of
the parenchyma and pancreatic duct margins (Table 1).
Grade I was defined as pancreas in which ⬎80% of the
parenchyma was hypoechoic or isoechoic when compared with the spleen, the main pancreatic duct was
clearly delineated, and fine, “salt and pepper” dots in the
pancreatic parenchyma were clearly seen. Grade II was
defined as pancreas in which ⬎80% of the parenchyma
was hyperechoic when compared with the spleen, the
main pancreatic duct was clearly delineated, and fine, salt
and pepper dots in the pancreatic parenchyma were
clearly seen. Grade III was defined as pancreas in which
⬎80% of the parenchyma was moderately more hyperechoic as compared with the spleen, the main pancreatic
duct margins were moderately obscured, and fine, salt and
pepper dots in the pancreatic parenchyma were moderately blurry. Grade IV was defined as pancreas in which
⬎80% of the parenchyma was severely more hyperechoic
when compared with the spleen, the pancreas could not
be separated from the adjacent fat, the main pancreatic
duct margins were severely obscured, and fine, salt and
pepper dots in the pancreatic parenchyma were severely
obscured. When pancreatic mass lesions or cysts were
present, grading required ⬎80% of the uninvolved parenchyma. Grades I and II were considered normal pancreas,
whereas grades III and IV were considered fatty pancreas
(Fig. 1). Hepatic echogenicity was also prospectively
graded I through IV in comparison to the spleen: grade I,
liver hypoechoic as compared with the spleen; grade II,

During the study period, 250 consecutive patients were
prospectively enrolled, of which 230 underwent grading

of pancreatic echogenicity during EUS examination. In 20
patients, the pancreas was not graded: in 10 patients the
pancreas was not examined because only a focused examination was conducted to minimize procedure duration
for clinical reasons. In 4 patients, altered surgical anatomy
limited adequate visualization of the pancreas. In 4 patients, an EUS miniprobe was used instead of a linear or
radial array echoendoscope. In these patients, the decision
to use the miniprobe was made after the onset of the
procedure. In 2 patients the pancreas was completely
replaced by cysts, thus limiting parenchymal evaluation.
Baseline patient characteristics are summarized in Table
2. Mean (⫾ standard deviation) age was 62.9 ⫾ 13.9 years,
mean BMI was 27.4 ⫾ 6.8 kg/m2, and 53.6% of study
participants were female. Comorbidities included hyperlipidemia (55.6%), hypertension (52.8%), diabetes (22.8%),
history of acute pancreatitis (19.6%), pancreatic adenocarcinoma (13.6%), and chronic pancreatitis (7.6%). Study
criteria for the metabolic syndrome were met by 14.8% of
patients. The most common indications for EUS were assessment of pancreatic mass or cyst (38%), biliary abnormalities (13.2%), submucosal mass in the upper GI tract
(12.8%), and esophageal mass/nodule (10%). Other indications included history of idiopathic acute pancreatitis
(6.8%), abdominal pain of unknown cause (3.6%), fiducial
placement (3.2%), gastric cancer staging (2.8%), ampullary
cancer staging (2.0%), pancreatic cancer screening in patients with familial pancreatitis (2.0%), and celiac plexus
neurolysis (1.2%).
Of the 230 patients who underwent grading of pancreatic fat, fatty pancreas was seen in 64 patients (27.8%, 95%
confidence interval [CI], 22.1-34.1). Grade III fatty pancreas was seen in 57 of 230 patients (24.8%, 95% CI,
19.3-30.9), whereas grade IV fatty pancreas was seen in 7
of 230 patients (3.0%, 95% CI, 1.2-6.2). The pancreas was
normal in the remaining 72.4% of patients (grade I ⫽
7.8%, grade II ⫽ 64.3%). The prevalence of fatty pancreas by age is shown in Table 3. Hepatic steatosis was
present in 22.6% of patients. Endosonographer 1 found
fatty pancreas in 33 of 134 patients, whereas endosonographer 2 found fatty pancreas in 31 of 96 patients (24.6% versus 32.3%; P ⫽ .26).

Before data collection, the study team reviewed classification with endosonographers by using multiple EUS images
of the pancreas, liver, and spleen. Classification also was
displayed next to the EUS processor when study EUS cases
were performed. This study was approved by our institutional review board.

Statistics
For sample size calculation, we assumed a 20% prevalence of fatty pancreas in our patient population. We
planned to allow for up to 5 factors in our final multivariate regression model. So as not to overfit our regression
model, we used the rule of thumb of 8 “outcomes” per
explanatory variable. This required that we enroll 200
patients to have at least 40 patients with fatty pancreas.
Therefore, we chose to enroll 250 patients in our study.
Quantitative data are summarized by the mean and
standard deviation. Univariate analysis was performed by
using fatty pancreas as the outcome variable. Predictor
variables included patient age, which was modeled as
both continuous and dichotomous variables (age ⬍50 and
ⱖ50 years); BMI, which was modeled as both continuous
and dichotomous variables (obese and nonobese); tobacco use, which was modeled as pack years of smoking;
and ethanol use, which was modeled as the ethanol index.
Dichotomous predictor variables included male sex, history of hyperlipidemia, hypertension, pancreatic cancer,
acute pancreatitis, chronic pancreatitis, the presence of
fatty liver, and the metabolic syndrome. A multivariate
logistic regression model was then created by using fatty
pancreas as the outcome variable. Predictor variables with
a P value of ⬍ .10 on univariate analysis were entered into
the model.

Factors associated with fatty pancreas on univariate
analysis were the metabolic syndrome (odds ratio [OR]
3.13, P ⫽ .004), BMI (OR 1.06, P ⫽ .004), hyperlipidemia
(OR 1.90, P ⫽ .04), and fatty liver (OR 4.12, P ⬍ .0001)
(Table 4). When we counted the number of metabolic
syndrome parameters (0 to 4; BMI ⱖ30, hyperlipidemia,
diabetes, hypertension), an increasing number of parameters was associated with an increasing prevalence of fatty
pancreas (OR 1.37, P ⫽ .01 for trend) (Fig. 2). Patients with
all 4 metabolic syndrome parameters had a 40% prevalence of fatty pancreas. Obese patients (BMI ⱖ30) were
2.5 times more likely to have fatty pancreas than patients
who were not obese (BMI ⬍30). Patients with hyperlipidemia were almost twice as likely to have fatty pancreas

when compared with those without hyperlipidemia. Fatty
liver was present in 42.2% of patients with fatty pancreas.
There was a trend toward association with hypertension,
although this was not statistically significant (OR 1.71, P ⫽
.08). There did not appear to be an association between
pancreatic cancer and fatty pancreas. The prevalence of
pancreatic cancer in patients with fatty pancreas was
10.6%, whereas the prevalence was 15.0% in patients without fatty pancreas (P ⫽ .42). There was also no association
with age, tobacco or alcohol use, diabetes, or acute or
chronic pancreatitis. Lipase levels were available within 1
year of the EUS examination for 74 of 230 patients,
whereas 58 of 230 patients had amylase levels available.
Lipase (OR 0.99, P ⫽ .21) and amylase (OR 0.99, P ⫽ .37)
levels were not associated with fatty pancreas.

DISCUSSION

Factors associated with fatty pancreas on multivariate
analysis were fatty liver (OR 3.61, P ⫽ .0002) and BMI (OR
1.05, P ⫽ .03) (Table 5). The risk of fatty pancreas increased by 5% for every 1 kg/m2 increase in BMI. The
metabolic syndrome could not be entered into the multivariable regression model because it includes components
of BMI, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes and
therefore was not an independent predictor variable. In
post hoc analysis, a second regression model was created
by using only grade IV fatty pancreas (severe fatty infiltra-

By virtue of its location in the retroperitoneum, the
pancreas is notoriously difficult to image by using conventional radiological techniques. The pancreas cannot be
fully imaged with transabdominal US because of overlying
air in the stomach and small intestine. CT scans can be
used to image the pancreas in its entirety, but CT is inaccurate in measuring pancreatic fat. Pancreatic fat deposits
primarily in the interlobular septa. This results in a heterogeneous pattern on CT scans, making determination of
tissue density (fat) by using Hounsfield units unreliable.7,18
Because it allows placing the US transducer in close proximity to the pancreas parenchyma, EUS can provide detailed images of the entire pancreas. The use of highfrequency US waves and the ability to simultaneously
image adjacent organs like the liver and spleen in real-time

Evaluation of fatty pancreas by using EUS

Sepe et al

makes EUS an excellent modality to study pancreas fat.
The grading system used in our study was adapted from
previous grading systems used by Marks et al7 and
Worthen and Beabeau.9 In these grading systems, the
pancreas was compared with the liver. Grade I was given
when echogenicity of the pancreas equaled that of the
liver. Grade II was given when echogenicity was slightly
greater than that of the liver. Grade III was given when
echogenicity was definitely greater than that of the liver.
Grade IV was given when echogenicity was the same as
that of retroperitoneal fat. Unfortunately, this system is
limited because the liver itself may have increasing echogenicity with fat. To overcome this, Al-Haddad et al10 used
both the liver and spleen as reference organs, whereas Lee
et al12 used the kidney. All of these systems have limitations, in that they rely on subjective descriptions of
“slightly greater” and “definitely greater.” Thus, in our
grading scheme (Table 1), we settled on assessment of
echogenicity as previously done, but we also used a more
detailed look at clarity of the parenchyma and pancreatic
duct margins. Because the normal pancreas can be hyperechoic as compared with the liver, spleen, and kidney,
these additional factors were important to distinguish between normal and abnormal echogenicity.
To our knowledge, the only other study that used EUS
to analyze fatty pancreas used a retrospective EUS image
database to identify 60 patients with fatty pancreas.10
When compared with age-matched and sex-matched controls, alcohol use in excess of 14 g/week, increasing BMI,
and hepatic steatosis were found to be associated with
fatty pancreas. Lee et al12 performed a retrospective review
of 293 patients in an obesity clinic by using transabdominal US images to grade pancreatic fat. Fatty pancreas was
seen in 61.4% of patients. Hemostatic model assessment of
insulin resistance, visceral fat, and alanine aminotransferase levels were independently related to fatty pancreas.
Saisho et al14 used CT scans to study pancreatic volume
and fat in children and adults. They found that during
childhood and adolescence, pancreas volume and fat
were associated with increasing age, whereas in adults
these were associated with increasing BMI.14 In our study,

we found no association between increasing age and
prevalence of fatty pancreas (Table 3). Most recently, Heni
et al11 evaluated 51 participants with magnetic resonance
imaging and found that pancreatic fat was associated with
BMI, visceral adipose tissue, and waist circumference but
not with fatty liver. Lingvay et al13 studied 79 patients with
magnetic resonance imaging and found that pancreatic
steatosis increases with BMI and impaired glycemia. Finally, Sijens et al15 demonstrated that pancreatic fat correlated with liver fat, and both are associated with BMI.
Interestingly, renal fat accumulation was not associated
with either BMI or fatty liver.
The results of these earlier studies along with those of
our study support the hypothesis that fatty pancreas is
part of the metabolic syndrome. Our study found a
higher prevalence of fatty pancreas in those patients
who met the definition of the metabolic syndrome when
compared with those who did not. Further, fatty pancreas was associated with individual components of the
metabolic syndrome and its associated entities. We
found a strong association between fatty pancreas and
BMI and fatty liver. Hyperlipidemia was associated on
univariate but not multivariate analysis. Hypertension
showed a trend toward an association, but this was not
statistically significant. This constellation of associations
suggests that fatty pancreas should be included in the
manifestations of the metabolic syndrome.
In our study, patients with fatty pancreas were more
than 3-fold more likely to meet the definition of the metabolic syndrome when compared with those without fatty
pancreas (OR 3.13, P ⫽ .004). In order to determine
whether the association between fatty pancreas and the
metabolic syndrome was mostly accounted for by increasing BMI, we studied the association between fatty pancreas and increasing number of metabolic syndrome parameters. The addition of every single metabolic syndrome
parameter (ie, BMI ⱖ30, diabetes, hypertension, or hypercholesterolemia) increased the risk of fatty pancreas by
37%. Interestingly, we found no independent association
between fatty pancreas and diabetes. This remained true
when we analyzed insulin-dependant and non-insulin–
dependant diabetes mellitus separately.
Fatty pancreas is strongly associated with fatty liver
and shares several risk factors. Although the pathophysiologic manifestations of fatty liver are well-understood,
it remains uncertain whether the presence of fat in the
pancreas has any deleterious health consequences. The
recognition of obesity as a risk factor for pancreatic
cancer, diabetes, and severe acute pancreatitis has led
some to suggest fatty infiltration of the pancreas as the
causal link. It is possible that pancreatic steatosis may
promote the development of chronic pancreatitis and
cancer, exacerbate the severity of acute pancreatitis,
increase the risk of pancreatic surgery, and lead to the
development of diabetes. We found no association between fatty pancreas and pancreatic cancer. Patients

with confirmed pancreatic cancer in our study were no
more likely to demonstrate fat in the portion of the
pancreas unaffected by neoplasia when compared with
others. It is possible that pancreatic fat could have
regressed due to effects of the local cytokine and inflammatory milieu from a nearby neoplasm or perhaps
from worsening nutritional status. In addition, pancreatic parenchyma upstream from a malignant pancreatic
mass can have associated atrophy and ductal dilation.
Our results also suggest that there may be an association
between acute recurrent pancreatitis and severe fatty
infiltration, although this association did not reach statistical significance in our study (P ⫽ .07). It should be
recognized that the presence of severe fatty pancreas
(grade IV) likely limited our ability to evaluate for EUS
criteria of chronic pancreatitis (lobularity, calcifications,
hyperechoic foci, hyperechoic strands) in 7 patients.
Several additional limitations of our study warrant further attention. Our study was performed at a tertiary-care
institution and enrolled a population of patients referred
for EUS. This may limit the generalizability of our findings.
We also did not have histological confirmation of fat infiltration of the pancreas. We assumed that increasing echogenicity was due to increasing fat content, based on studies of US in the evaluation of hepatic steatosis.19-21 In
addition, Marks et al7 demonstrated that fat is the major
determining factor of increasing echogenicity in the pancreas. Another study demonstrated that hypoechogenicity
in the pancreas is due to diminished fat content.22 Optimum assessment of fatty pancreas requires evaluation of
EUS images in real time. We were unable to have both
endosonographers present for every EUS examination.
Thus, we were unable to perform interobserver variability.
There was consistent agreement between endosonographers during the before-study review of classification and
teaching. Further, there was no significant difference in
percentage of patients with fatty pancreas as graded by the
two endosonographers. Four patients did have a repeat
EUS examination performed by a different endosonographer. In all 4 examinations, blinded grading was equivalent between the two endosonographers.
In conclusion, fatty pancreas was noted in 1 of 4 patients
undergoing EUS. Obesity, hepatic steatosis, and increasing
number of metabolic syndrome parameters were predictive
of fatty pancreas. This supports the hypothesis that fatty
pancreas is a manifestation of the metabolic syndrome.
